analysis.one_liner: Gives people crushed by medical bills easier bankruptcy terms, including keeping more home equity and erasing student loans.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; the Senate Judiciary Committee took no action after it was referred on the day of introduction, and it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change bankruptcy law for people whose finances collapsed because of medical bills. A "medically distressed" debtor — for example, someone who owed more than $10,000 in out-of-pocket medical costs over three years — could keep up to $250,000 of home value, skip the income screening and credit counseling course that normally gate bankruptcy filings, cancel student loans along with other debts, and pay less into court-supervised repayment plans. The bill was introduced in the Senate in November 2024, sent to the Judiciary Committee, and never taken up again.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose finances were wrecked by illness — their own or a family member's — would get an easier path through bankruptcy: they could keep up to $250,000 of home equity, skip the income-based screening that filters out many filers, skip the pre-filing credit counseling course, wipe out student loans alongside medical bills, and keep more income in a repayment plan. The definition reaches people who owed more than 10% of income (or $10,000) in medical bills over three years, lost income because of illness or caregiving, or lost child or spousal support because of a medical problem.

how_it_helps.text: Medically distressed debtors could exempt up to $250,000 in value in their home, co-op, or burial plot — the federal homestead exemption is currently far lower — so a family would not have to sell the house to pay medical bills.

The means test in Chapter 7 and the disposable-income rule in Chapter 13 would not apply to medically distressed debtors, letting them file Chapter 7 or keep more income in a repayment plan regardless of the formula.
Medically distressed debtors would be exempt from the pre-bankruptcy credit counseling requirement.
Medically distressed debtors could cancel student loans in bankruptcy without proving 'undue hardship,' the near-impossible standard that blocks most student debt discharge.
The definition covers people who lost wages or jobs because of their own illness, caring for a sick family member, or a declared public health emergency, and spouses of qualifying debtors.
Debtors must file a statement of medical expenses under penalty of perjury, declaring they did not incur expenses just to qualify.

analysis.who_pays: Creditors — including medical providers, credit card issuers, and debt collectors — would recover less from medically distressed debtors, since more debt would be discharged and more property shielded. The costs could ripple back to other borrowers through slightly higher lending costs, and the $250,000 home exemption could shift some recoveries away from creditors in high-home-value states.
analysis.who_pays_short: Creditors, including medical providers and lenders

drawbacks.text: The $250,000 home exemption is far above the current federal limit and is not means-tested beyond the medical-distress definition, so a filer with a high-value house and modest medical bills could shield substantial wealth from creditors.

The bill waives both the 2005 means test and the credit counseling requirement for this class of filers, undoing screening that Congress put in place to filter bankruptcy filings; critics of such carve-outs warn the costs get spread to other borrowers through higher lending prices.

Wiping out student loans for medically distressed debtors without the undue-hardship showing would forgive debts that some filers could have repaid, a cost borne by federal taxpayers and private lenders.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: medical debt is a leading driver of personal bankruptcy, and the bill's definition is reasonably tight (10% of income or $10,000 over three years, job loss from illness, with an anti-abuse attestation under penalty of perjury). The main costs fall on creditors rather than the general public, though the untested $250,000 home exemption is generous enough that it could let higher-asset filers shield wealth, and forgiving student debt without the undue-hardship showing has a real fiscal cost. The bill received no committee scrutiny, so none of these design questions were ever tested or refined.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never heard from again, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 21, 2024, with six Democratic cosponsors, in the final weeks of the two-year Congress.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day, and no further action was ever taken on it.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill expired without a hearing, a markup, or any vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Creditors, including medical providers and debt collectors, are better off because the bill died: they keep the full set of collection tools against people whose debts stem from illness. Americans with medical debt got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Creditors and collectors keep full leverage over sick debtors

for.name: Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee.

for.name: Sen. Blumenthal, Warren, Welch, Lujan, and Baldwin

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress; no hearings, markup, or floor vote occurred.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor after it sat in committee without action.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill was introduced and cosponsored only by Democrats in the Senate.

industries.note: The bill would wipe out more debt from medically distressed filers and shield more of their assets, so less money would flow to the companies and institutions that collect on medical and consumer debt.

industries.industry: Hospitals and medical providers as creditors
industries.note: Hospitals and doctors often hold unpaid medical bills; broader discharge protections and a higher home exemption would mean recovering less from patients who file for bankruptcy.

industries.industry: Healthcare billing and medical debt financing
industries.note: Medical debt would remain dischargeable as it is today, but the bill does not lower the underlying bills that cause medical bankruptcy in the first place.
